Something is instinctual when it comes from instinct — a natural, built-in drive or response that a living being is born with. It is not something taught, reasoned through, or consciously decided. It just happens, arising from somewhere deep inside, as if the body or mind already knew what to do before the brain had a chance to think.

To truly grasp "instinctual," you need to first understand instinct, because instinctual simply means "of, relating to, or arising from instinct."

An instinct is a natural, automatic pattern of behavior or feeling that is hardwired into a creature from birth. It is part of the biological and psychological makeup of a species. No one teaches it. No experience creates it. It is simply there from the very beginning.

For example: a newborn baby, within moments of birth, will turn its head and begin sucking when something touches its cheek. Nobody taught the baby this. The baby did not think, "I need food — I should search for it." The response fired on its own, automatically, from deep within. That is instinct. And because that sucking behavior arises from instinct, it is called instinctual.

The adjective instinctual is used to describe behaviors, urges, feelings, reactions, or responses that share these qualities: they are inborn rather than learned; they happen automatically, often without conscious thought; they are driven by biology or deep psychological wiring; and they are generally shared by all or most members of a species.

Here are some examples in sentences to make this concrete:

"A mother's instinctual urge to protect her child was so powerful that she ran toward the danger before she even realized what she was doing." — She did not stop to think or weigh her options. The urge came from somewhere far deeper than rational thought.

"The bird has an instinctual drive to migrate south when temperatures begin to drop." — No one trained the bird. It was born knowing when and where to go.

"He felt an instinctual sense of unease the moment he walked into the room, even though everything looked perfectly normal." — The feeling arose from some deep inner signal, not from logic or observation.

"Babies have an instinctual fear of falling, even before they have ever experienced a fall." — They are born with it already wired in.
What is instinctual versus what is not

This distinction is important. Instinctual things come from nature; non-instinctual things come from learning, culture, or conscious choice.

Instinctual: a baby crying when hungry, an animal fleeing when it senses a predator, the fight-or-flight surge of fear when you suddenly face danger, a parent's impulse to comfort a distressed child.

Not instinctual: speaking a language (learned), playing a musical instrument (learned), choosing what to eat for dinner (a conscious decision), being polite to strangers (socially taught). These involve thinking, training, or cultural influence.

The line between the two is not always perfectly sharp, though. Some behaviors are a blend of instinct and learning. Humans have an instinctual drive to communicate with others, for instance — but the specific language they speak is entirely learned. The drive is inborn; the expression of it is shaped by environment.
How "instinctual" is used loosely in everyday language

In strict scientific or psychological usage, instinctual refers only to truly inborn, unlearned behaviors. But in everyday conversation, people sometimes use it more loosely to describe anything that feels automatic, second-nature, or deeply intuitive — even if it was originally learned.

For example: "After twenty years of cooking, she instinctually knew how much salt the dish needed." Technically, that skill was built through experience, not born into her. But it has become so automatic and effortless that it feels like instinct. People speak this way all the time, and the meaning is clear from context. Just be aware that when used this way, the word is being used loosely rather than in its precise sense.

You will often encounter these two words side by side, and they are very frequently used as if they mean the same thing — and in most practical situations, they do. However, there is a subtle shade of difference worth knowing.

Instinctive tends to describe how something is done — naturally, automatically, without conscious effort. ("He instinctively ducked when he heard the bang.") It emphasizes the manner of the action.

Instinctual tends to describe what something is by nature — its origin, its character, its relationship to instinct. ("An instinctual need for safety." "Instinctual behavior in animals.") It emphasizes belonging to or arising from instinct as a phenomenon.

That said, most dictionaries and most writers treat them as interchangeable, and you will rarely go wrong using either one. The distinction matters more in academic or psychological writing than in everyday use.

Whenever you encounter the word instinctual, ask yourself this simple question: Did this arise from nature — from being born wired this way — or did it come from learning, choice, or conscious thought? If the answer is nature, the word fits perfectly. The salmon swimming upstream to spawn is not following a map — it is following something ancient and inborn. That is instinctual. A student memorizing a map to navigate a city is not — that is learned.

Instinctual means arising from, rooted in, or belonging to instinct — the natural, automatic, inborn drives and responses that exist within a living being independent of learning or reasoning. It is the opposite of deliberate, learned, or reasoned. When something is instinctual, nature did the programming; life experience had nothing to do with it.
